`return parseTexFiles(Collections.singletonList(texFile));` should be sufficient (see below for the issue concerning `add`).
I think there is no need to have seperate `parse` and `parseTexFiles` methods.

Please use a for loop. Instead of updating the `texFiles` with new files, I would prefer a recursive approach: parse the given files and make a list of all referenced latex files, then parse these files (repeating as long as necessary) and finally return the combined results.
Personally, I would split parsing the latex file and cross-referencing it with a given `BibDatabase` (it is a bit more flexible and in the spirit of "each class does only one job")

In general, it is better to create the expected result (here: `TexParserResult`) and then compare it in one `assertEquals` statement. To see why: change your implementation so that some of the tests fail, and then try to guess the source of the failure from the test output.

Thanks! Now it supports many citation commands, even though multicite commands are not ready yet.
All database-related methods are now in another class, but I still have to make some changes within the following days.

Tests for the crossreferencing should be in another class (CrossingKeysTest). With unit tests, you want to test each element in isolation, i.e. parser extracts correct citation and crossing keys assigns correct entries.
It is also good to have a few more global tests that make sure the whole process works (these are called integration tests), but these should be in a separate testclass.

Please try not to build the database based on a bib file but by hand using `BibDatabase database = ...`, `BibEntry entry = new Entry(...).withField(...)` and `database.insertEntry(...)`. Preferable you only need to this once in the `setup` method of the test class and then reuse it across the tests.

If you need to introduce helper methods in the test class, then this is usually a sign that the class under test needs to be refactored/extended to allow a better interaction.
For example, why not add a `addCitation(String key, Path file, ...)` method directly in `TexParserResult`?
Personally, I would inline this method in `testMatchCite` and `testNonMatchCite` since the code duplication is essentially only 2 lines.

From what I see this could be converted to the "normal" advanced for. eg. for(Path file: textFiles) or do you really need the index(position information somewhere?

Do we really need to clone the entry? That is usually not necessary and might lead to confusions (e.g. when you modify the cloned entry without realizing that it is a clone and thus does not affect the original entry).

original_comments: Please don't change this, but instead use `getShortName` in the exporters

Although this change makes sense to me and we might change the logic to your version in the future, I would prefer if we don't touch parsing and writing of latex files as part of this PR. There are just too many things that can go wrong and we don't have extensive tests in place to capture them.

Thus, please keep the current behavior here (`month = jan` is stored as `#jan#` in BibEntry; moreover, `#jan#` should be written as `month = jan`).

I think, this logic is also used to handle string constants (see https://tex.stackexchange.com/a/303489/9075), so we should be very cautious when touching this.

In short: A user should be able to enter a reference to a constant. 

* BibTex:  `Journal = IEEE_M_COM` <-> entry editor: `#IEEE_M_COM#`
* BibTex:  `Journal = {IEEE_M_COM}` <-> entry editor: `IEEE_M_COM`

This is a "quick hack" existing since the early days of JabRef. No one came up with another solution. Especially when joining constants with "real" text: BibTex: `Journal = IEEE_M_COM # {some more text}`

This would disable the button when recent libraries are empty, but I don't see any code that would re-enable it when recent library item is added.

I assume that `FileHistoryMenu#newFile(Path file)` [invocation](https://github.com/JabRef/jabref/blob/main/src/main/java/org/jabref/gui/importer/actions/OpenDatabaseAction.java?plain=1#L159) within the `OpenDatabaseAction` class, will re-enable the item as the aforementioned method declares : `setDisable(false)`. To my understanding, the menu `Recent Libraries` shall be disabled unless the user opens a library.

I also tested it manually and the system's behavior is as expected. When we open a new library the `Recent libraries` menu will be correctly enabled and the recent libraries will be listed.
